title: Cassandra in depth
subtitle: Cassandra makes writes cheap and pays later, in compaction, tombstones and repair. Learn where each cost lands, so deleted data stays deleted and reads stay fast.

c.v: Uber runs Cassandra as an internal service. In 2023 it had tens of thousands of nodes and tens of millions of

Teams that used it reported a strange problem: "data inconsistency due to data resurrection". Data they had deleted came back. Uber's write-up names the usual causes: "Frequent data deletions and downed nodes".
The fix was repair, the background job that makes
agree. Uber's repairs were slow. Its
With Cassandra's default grace period of 10 days, a repair that takes tens of days cannot keep up.
Uber's post does not say which grace period it used.
So Uber made repair part of Cassandra itself, like
. It works through the ring node by node and needs no outside
. The p99 repair time fell to "just under a single-digit number of days".
Some use cases that relied heavily on

saw higher error rates "every other week". The cause was in node replacement. The new node kept looking up the old node's hostname. When that lookup failed, its view of pending ring changes no longer matched the other nodes.
None of this is a bug in your queries. It is how Cassandra stores and deletes data. This lesson shows the parts you must run yourself.
You already know two halves of Cassandra.
This lesson joins them. Cassandra never changes a file on disk. So a delete cannot remove data. It writes a marker instead, a
Every replica must see that marker before any replica throws it away.
In Cassandra, a delete is a write that must reach every replica before its grace period ends. Compaction cleans up, and repair makes sure there is nothing left to bring back. You must run both well.
A write first goes to a commit log on disk, added at the end. Then it goes into the memtable in memory.
By default the commit log uses "periodic" sync. The write is acknowledged at once, and the log is synced every 10 seconds. A crash can lose up to that period, or more if a sync is late.
When the memtable is full, Cassandra flushes it to a new SSTable. That file is never written again. So one
is usually spread over several SSTables.
A read must merge the memtable and every SSTable that may hold the partition.
. It says "surely not here" or "maybe here", so most files are skipped.
For a file that may have it, a partition index points to the data's place in the file.
The read keeps the newest value for each cell, by timestamp. A tombstone hides every older value.
So a read for live rows must still step over tombstones.
The default false-positive chance is 0.01 for most tables and 0.1 for leveled ones. Going from 0.1 to 0.01 roughly triples the filter's memory.
Step through one delete. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The grace period is the table setting
. Its default is 864000 seconds, which is 10 days.
After that, compaction may drop the tombstone. It needs every older SSTable for that partition in the same compaction.
By default, Cassandra does not run repair for you.
Since 5.0.8 it has a built-in scheduler, Auto Repair, but you must turn it on.
With the default grace period, the docs say to repair every node at least once every 7 days.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: For each table, write down how rows die: delete, TTL, or never. Pick the compaction strategy from that answer.
Alert when repair has not finished on every node within the grace period. Missing it is silent until data comes back.
Watch tombstone warnings in the logs. Each one names a query that scans too much.
Before a design review, ask, "Does any read step over many deleted rows?" Queues, inboxes and "latest status" tables are the usual suspects.
Use lightweight transactions only where a race costs money or trust, such as unique usernames. Measure their
on every node in a data centre. A new node with a different value owns a different share of data.
"Here is our Cassandra schema and every query. For each table, tell me how rows are removed, the compaction strategy you would pick, and why. Flag any table that behaves like a queue."
"Write a test on a 3-node cluster. Stop one node, delete a row, set gc_grace_seconds to 60, compact the others, start the node and run repair. Show whether the row comes back."
"Find every counter update and IF condition in this code. For each, say what happens on a timeout and a retry."

q.v: You delete a row at QUORUM while one replica is down for two days. Nobody runs repair. Twelve days later, the row appears again. The table uses the default gc_grace_seconds. What happened?

options.v: Compaction on the other replicas dropped the tombstone after 10 days. Then the down replica's old copy looked like live data and was copied back.
The QUORUM delete was rolled back because one replica failed.
The row's TTL reset itself when the replica came back.

why.v: A tombstone can be purged after gc_grace_seconds, 10 days by default. A replica that never got it still has the row, and nothing remains to say it was deleted.

q.v: Your table stores sensor readings with a 30-day TTL. Rows are never updated or deleted by hand. Which compaction strategy do the Cassandra docs design for this?

why.v: The docs say TWCS is designed for TTL'ed, mostly immutable time-series data. When a whole window expires, Cassandra can drop the SSTable instead of merging it.

q.v: A jobs table works like a queue. Workers read the oldest rows in one partition and delete them when done. After a few weeks, reads slow down and logs warn about tombstones. Why?

options.v: Deleted rows are removed at once, so the partition gets too small.
Each delete leaves a tombstone. A read for the oldest live rows must scan past every tombstone still in the partition.

why.v: Deletes are writes. Tombstones stay for at least gc_grace_seconds, and a scan keeps the ones it sees in memory. That is why cassandra.yaml has warn and failure thresholds.

q.v: A counter update times out. Your code retries it. What can happen?

options.v: Nothing bad. Counter updates are idempotent.
The counter may count the update twice, because the first try may have been applied.
Cassandra rejects the retry with a duplicate error.

why.v: The docs say counter updates are not idempotent. After a timeout the client cannot know if the update was applied, so replaying it may over count.

q.v: Why did Cassandra 4.0 lower the default num_tokens from 256 to 16?

options.v: Fewer tokens means less memory for Bloom filters.
With a smarter token allocator, a few tokens per node spread data well. Many tokens tie many nodes together, which raises the risk of unavailability.
Because 16 is the largest value the Murmur3 partitioner accepts.

why.v: The docs say a high token count couples many nodes together. The deterministic allocator added in 3.x lets nodes use far fewer tokens.
